It shows that animals and meats, fourteen commodities, as compared with the decade from 1890 to 1899 increased tin price by forty-eight per cent and as compared with 1898, which was the last year of the Conservative Administration, by eighty per cent. In fish, the increase compared with the decade from 1890 to 1899 was thirty-four per cent, and as compared with 1896, thirty-one per cent. In other foods-thirty-seven commodities were taken-the increase was seven per cent compared with the decade from 1890 to 1899 and twenty-two per cent as compared wiith 1896. It seems perfectly clear then that, upon the figures given by the Labour Gazette, confirmed as they are by this statement filed by the Minister of Labour in Sir Wilfrid Laurier's Government, during the years of the Liberal Administration this was a live question, discussed publiicly and privately, and considered to be a worthy subject of legislation in this House. The Hon. Mr. King continued :
Throughout the Dominion the steady increase in the cost of living, especially since the beginning of the present century, haa been the subject of repeated comment, and, In almost every city or centre of employment, of more or less careful examination. In 1906 the Ontario Educational Association went carefully into the whole matter, in connection with the arrangement of teachers' salaries, with the result that an increase amounting to thirty per cent in ten years was shown. In 1907 an estimate made by the Synod of the Church of England in the city of Quebec placed the increase within the decade at a much higher rate.
The House will observe that all these bodies were considering this question.
In the city of Toronto, an investigation conducted with care and minuteness during 1907, by the Department of Political Economy of the University of Toronto, also showed a higher rate of increase. These examples could be multiplied.
All show upward movement since 1896; 30 to 35 per cent higher average, 1890-99; 40 to 45 per cent higher average, 1896-97.
The cost of living has increased from 30 to 40 per cent, in the case of incomes ranging from $2,000 down to $500. That is a fact

which has impressed itself upon all classes of the community. We find the increase in the cost of living going on simultaneously with the organization of capital on a large scale, the formation of trusts, mergers and combines of one kind or another.
Let me point out, therefore, to my right hon. friend that this question, far from never having been raised during the fifteen years of his administration, was a live issue and was made the subject of legislation by his own Government. It was on account of the high cost of living that his minister was introducing the Combines Investigation Bill as a sovereign remedy. That was the remedy of my right hon. friend, not the abolition of customs duties. That was never suggested by my right hon. friend when the debate took place in the House. Many members on that occasion participated in the debate, among others the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald). He was not sure about this Combines Investigation legislation. He raised doubts about it, as appears from the report of his speech in ' Hansard.' So far as I know, there was only one man in the House who was true to the traditions of free trade and who raised his voice and stated that the high cost of living was due to the tariff. That was the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark). He was true to his free trade principles. It is true,-he has not always been consistent. He apostatized last session on the Naval Bill when he wanted the ships built here instead of at Glasgow. He denied the free trade policy on that occasion; but it is not on record that, like Peter, he went out and wept bitterly. On the' contrary, he rather gloried in it.
I have pointed out that my right hon. friend never suggested at that time'that the tariff was the cause of the increased cost of living. Of course he could not do so. His Finance Minister would not have let him. Let me illustrate what I mean for the benefit of my right hon. friend, who is going to abolish all duties on all foods-not only on farm products but manufactured articles as well. How can my right hon. friend argue that the tariff is the cause of the increased cost of living when the tariff upon the natural products of Canada has remained stationary for about twenty years?
I have taken the trouble to look up the rates of duty on foodstuffs since 1890. I am not going to weary the House by reading this table, but it shows clearly that on butter the tariff has remained stationary or been slightly reduced under the British preferential, at four cents a pound until the revision of the tariff by the Finance Minister of my right hon. friend at the time the
.
Labour Gazette was pointing out the high cost of living. The same remark applies to cheese, the duty on which was three cents a pound in 1890 and lower in 1907 under the customs tariff of to-day. The duty on eggs in 1894 was five cents a dozen and in 1907 three cents a dozen, and so on down the line. I make the statement that upon all these items that enter largely into the question of the high cost of living the tariff has remained constant for twenty years. It is perfectly clear, therefore, that the tariff is not the cause of the increased cost of living.
We come now to a rather perplexing problem. As my right hon. friend has offered no explanation, we must do a little guessing. What is the explanation of the new fiscal policy put forth by my right hon. friend, not in the House of Commons, although he referred to it yesterday, but put forward at Hamilton as the policy which he gave the people for the present? Why this sudden interest on his part in the consumer? I think the explanation lies in the attitude that my right hon. friend took on the question of reciprocity. I had hoped that I should not have again to discuss this question in the House, but it appears from what my hon. friend from Red Deer said last night that there is a grave difference of opinion between himself and his leader as to the condition of reciprocity at the present time. My right hon. friend in his Hamilton speech said, speaking of reciprocity: Let the dead past bury its dead. My hon. friend from Red Deer dropped a rather cryptic utterance last night. He said: Reciprocity in its old form will not be with us again, but it is not dead. My hon. friend from Red Deer must be a political Buddhist, believing in reincarnation. He evidently believes in the transmigration, not of souls, but of reciprocity pacts. Now, I regard my hon. friend as not only a very able debater but as a physician of some distinction.
I am beginning to entertain some doubts of his capacity as a physician, because it has taken him two years to find out what is the undoubted fact-and he has not even found it out yet-that reciprocity is dead. My hon. friend said last night that reciprocity was now 50 per cent, in operation. I think we shall find in that statement the explanation of the free food policy of my right hon. friend. He desires that the other 50 per cent, shall come into operation. My right hon. friend will remember that when the reciprocity treaty

was under consideration in this House, there was no suggestion, so far as I have been able to learn from his speeches, that any benefit would inure to the consumer. Let me read to my right hon. friend what he said in the House of Commons on that [DOT]occasion. He said:
One object to-day is to open the door of a nation of 90,000,000 which has been closed to us	I stated a moment ago that the agreement we made, is simply to get better prices for the product of the Canadian farmers. This is a proposition so obvious that I am surprised it should have received the treatment it has received on the part of our friends opposite.
The point I wish to make is that my right hon. friend had not the consumer in mind at all at that time. To clinch that argument, let us see what my right hon. friend did. It was pointed out that the farmer would not get as much benefit as appeared upon the surface, and that by reason of the operation of the most favoured nation treaties the markets of Canada would be opened to the farm products of the thirteen most favoured nations. That argument was put forward, it had some weight, and my right hon. friend thought it worth While to meet it. At the Imperial Conference in June, 1911, my right hon' 'friend presented jthe following resolution, which was adopted:
That His Majesty's Government be requested to open negotiations with the several Foreign Governments having treaties which apply to the Overseas Dominions with a view to securing libetry for any of those Dominions which may so desire to withdraw from the operation of the treaty without impairing the treaty in respect of the rest of the empire.
What	objection	had	my	right hon.friend	at that	time,	in	view of thehigh	cost of	living	that prevailedthen-and if he had any objection, is it	consistent	with	his	course now?-to	these thirteen most favoured
nations having access to the markets of Canada in the interest of the consumer? His position at the present time, in view of this agitation as to the high cost of living, and in view of the Combines Investigation Bill, introduced as a sovereign remedy by his minister, is not consistent with his position then. It is not consistent that at the present time he should advocate the abolition of duties when at that time he was bending all his energies not only against the abolition of duties but to prevent the most favoured nations from having free entry to the markets of Canada in the interests of the consumer. I just leave my right hon. friend to think it over as to why he did that.
During the process of that campaign an argument was developed that, as far as I know, had never been heard before, in order to catch the city and town vote. It was put forward that under reciprocity the farmer would get more for his products and the city dweller would pay less; that is to say, that a farmer living ten or twelve miles out of Ottawa would receive more for his butter and eggs and that a citizen of Ottawa, buying his butter and eggs, would pay less. That puzzled a great number of people in Canada, but it was put forward as an argument, and I do not see how the Liberal party can refuse to continue to argue that. As the tariff can have absolutely no bearing whatever upon the increased cost of living, one possible explanation of the fiscal policy of my right hon. friend is that he desires to bring the other half of reciprocity into operation. He hopes that by his persistency he may ultimately bring it about that we shall have reciprocity between Canada and the United States. We pointed out in that campaign that the farmer in Canada would retain his home markets, which are his steady and stable markets, and his best markets, and that he would, in the process of time, get access to the markets of the United States. To a large extent that position has been confirmed. The Underwood Tariff Bill does open the market of the United States to a very great number of the products of Canada, and the farmers of Canada at the same time have their home market, which they showed by their votes in 1911 they so much appreciated and valued.
Let us see what a free food policy means. My own view is that free food means free trade. I believe that, carried out to its logical conclusion, it is a reversal of the policy under which, during the time of my right hon. friend and of preceding governments, this country has prospered for the last forty years. I believe that it involves a reversal of that policy. A quotation given by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister last night showed that my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition had referred to the protection policy as bondage. Well, in the words of Abraham Lincoln, if it is bondage, I do not believe that the people will consent to be half bond and half free. This Government believes in that reasonable protection where required-believes in a reasonable protection for the industries of Canada in order that her industries may be developed and her home market built up. We believe in protection, and a reasonable pro-

tective policy is one that we feel should include not only the industries of Canada, so called-that is to say, the manufacturing industries-but that it should, in so far as may be necessary, include also the farmers. That has been the policy ever since 1878 and that was the policy in the United States until this year. We are fond of making comparisons between Canada and the United States, but we forget that the United States has has almost a century's start of us, that she has a hundred million of population, that specialized industries have been built up for generations and that it is not fair to compare these two countries as if they were on all fours. Because a certain policy is satisfactory to the United States and suits the people of the United States, it does not necessarily follow that that policy would suit the people of Canada with our population and at our stage of development. I think that very often men with the best of intentions make a mistake in jumping to the conclusion that whatever policy is adopted in the United States is necessarily good for Canada.
Now I come to the end of this discussion as far as I am concerned, as to the increased cost of living. What is the remedy for it ? It is perfectly clear that the abolition of customs duties is not the remedy. That is not going to change the trend upward of the cost of living, because, as I pointed out at the beginning of my remarks, this phenomenon is not confined to Canada. We find it in protectionist countries, we find it in free trade countries, we find it on the continent of America, on the continent of Europe, in Great Britain- it is a universal phenomenon. The solution is not in the abolition of customs duties. What is the solution ? I pointed out to the House that, according to comparative statistics between this country and New Zealand and Australia, we were not raising sufficient cattle, sheep and. swine in Canada. The most practical way to meet this question of the high cost of living-because it is involved with the consideration mentioned by the hon. member for North Oxford more than any other and with the trend cityward-the two are involved together-is to increase the production in Canada. That is the solution of the high cost of living problem-increased production. In Canada for many years we have been in this position that the trend cityward has been such that in the last decade between 1901 and 1911 the urban population increased sixty per cent and rural Canada increased only seventeen per cent, with a decline in Ontario, or a very slight increase-I forget which-I
,
think a decline-and in the Maritime provinces only seventeen per cent of an increase in the rural population and a sixty per cent increase in the urban population at a time when we were getting immigration at the rate of a thousand or twelve hundred a day and at a time when we have large undertakings under construction employing an army of men, all consumers. Yet, we have a declining rural population. What is the remedy ? The remedy is unquestionably increased production. . That is my view-I am speaking only for myself.
How are you going to increase it ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We will come to that. The way not to increase it is to disregard the interests of agriculture, as my right hon. friend did from 1896 to 1911. I am going to show precisely what was done. If a fraction of the money that has been spent upon the National Transcontinental between Moncton and Cochrane had been spent for agriculture, I do not believe this question of the high cost of living would have been to the front to-day. There is an overlapping jurisdiction in agriculture between the Dominion and the provinces.
I asked my department to prepare a statement as to the expenditure upon agriculture for the past four or five years, just in order to get a comparison between the two Administrations in the matter of agriculture. What do I find? I have the items here, and I intend to place them upon ' Hansard.' The total expenditure upon agriculture in 1910-11 was $1,192,417.13. In 1911-12 it had risen to $1,489,973.46. In 1912-13, the first year that we were in power, the expenditure had been increased to $2,436,103, and in 1913-14 we spent more than double the amount that was spent in 1910, namely, $2,630,500. That is not by any means all that this Government has done to promote agriculture.

What
has been the result?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Did my hon. friend hear
the eloquent address of my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) last night? If not, he missed a treat. My hon. friend from Red Deer said: Give it time for operation. The impatience of my hon. friend surprises me sometimes. A Bill was introduced last session by my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell), one of the most important measures, one of the most statesmanlike measures ever introduced into this House, setting aside the sum of $10,000,000, at the rate of $1,000,000

a year for the promotion of agricultural education throughout Canada. I shall be much surprised if that Bill does not produce very substantial results, just as soon as it is possible for it to get into operation, taking agricultural instruction to the farmer, teaching him as to his soils, as to his grains, as to his breeds of cattle. At all events that is a statesmanlike measure. A government that does that is doing something to promote agriculture. Therefore we have expenditures in the Estimates of 191314 of $2,630,500; and, notwithstanding the financial stringency, the Estimates of the coming year for agriculture aTe going to be greater than that. Notwithstanding that increased expenditure, there is $1,000,000 a year set aside for ten years. Whatever money is required by the Minister of Agriculture for the purposes of promoting husbandry throughout Canada, the raising of cattle, the raising of grain, is going to be supplied, so far at all events, as I can supply it. Therefore, in our humble way we have done something to deal with this question of the high cost of living by increasing production in Canada, because I think that is the very gist of the question, to increase production in Canada, to make farm life more agreeable, to make it brighter, to make it more attractive, to counteract the lure of the city and to make it more profitable. Let me ask my right hon. friend this question: how are you going to increase the attractiveness of farming, how are you going to appeal to the farmer's boy to stay on the farm, if you cut down the price of his product? The object of my right hon. friend, as I understand it, by abolishing customs duties upon food, is to cheapen farm products, eggs, butter, cattle, swine, sheep. Is that going to be a sovereign remedy? Will that appeal to the farmer if he gets less for his products? Will it? I ask that question.
I think that concludes that branch of the subject as to the high cost of living, brought into the discussion of my right hon. friend, and the fiscal policy which he announces as the policy of the Opposition -free food-that is to say, the abolition of all custom duties upon natural products and manufactured products constituting food.
The tariff has been somewhat under discussion in this debate upon the Address, although I entirely agree with my hon. friend from Red Deer, who fairly observes the rules of thtis House-in fact, who is somewhat of a stickler for the observance
of its rules-that this is not a Budget occasion, and consequently it is not the time, properly speaking, to discuss questions of the tariff. I am not suggesting for a moment that it is not in order, because any question can be dtiscussed in connection with the - debate upon the Address, either on the ground that it is not in the Speech from the Throne, or that it ought to be in the Speech from the Throne. While that is acknowledged, it is a fact that the proper hime for a debate upon the tariff is when the Bud et is brought down. My hon. friend from Red Deer is a consistent free trader, wit.i one notable exception of backsliding, to which I shall not refer again; because I can imagine that he might be sensitive about it. After all, one fall after a long consistent course of adherence to conviction should not be imputed too harshly to a man.
Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM:	Speaking personally?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, I am always willing to apply a rule to myself, but when I supported my right hon. friend he was a good protechionist. My hon. friend from Red Deer eulogizes and I join in the eulogy, Woodrow Wilson, the President of the United States as a great man. I join sincerely in that tribute to President Wilson. It gives me great pleasure to associate myself in the admiration of my hon. friend from Red De:r for the great head of our neighbouring republic. I have so expressed myself upon previious occasions. My hon. friend from Red Deer is nothing if not vigorous, and he told us last night in the most picturesque and forceful language how President Wilson has taken the American protective system and torn it up by the roots and scattered it to the four winds of heaveh. Those were his words.
I am sure my hon. frtiend will allow me. My recollection is that I said he had taken protectionist heresies, not the system. It would take time to take the system.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not quite see how it is possible to separate the heresies from the system. I do not believe my hon. friend quite, realizes what is involved in that statement. President Woodrow Wilson is the President who has brought about the revision of the American tariff under the terms of the Underwood Bill. And, in order that

my hon. friend may see just how far he has ' torn up ' either the protectionist system or the protectionist heresies, I want to point out to him that the rate of duties upon dutiable articles in Canada at the present time is under 26 per cent, and I will read to the House what Mr. Underwood, who introduced this Bill, said with regard to its effect upon the tariff of the United States. That will enable the House to see how far he has ' torn up ' the whole fabric of protection-although my hon. friend from Bed Deer did not use that term. This is from the Congressional Record of September last:
With few exceptions the House agreed to the Senate reductions.'^ The Senate receded on about one-half of the raises that it made in the Bill, with the result that the Bill as it is now presented to the House, as ascertained by the calculations made by the experts, will reach an average of about 26 per cent-almost as low as the famous Walker Bill, which carried a low tax on liquor and tobacco-and the tax on liquor and tobacco raises the average of this Bill very much.
I see an estimate in the London Times as to the average rate upon dutiable goods entering the United States under the new tariff, ana that estimate was that it was 29 per cent-three points higher than the figure named by the parent of the Underwood Bill. The point I desire to make is that my hon. friend from Red Deer is filled with admiration for the President of the United States for tearing up these protectionist heresies because he has brought about a situation in the United States unde-which their tariff is higher than that of Canada to-day, and yet the hon. gentleman is opposed to the tariff of Canada because it is a protectionist tariff. That
9 p.m. seems to me to be a reductio ad absurdum.
What are the respective tariffs of the two countries on agricultural implements?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: At present agricultural implement in Canada-that is, the principal agricultural implements such as binders, reapers, mowers and harvesters-pay 174 per cent. Under the reciprocity agreement negotiated by my predecessor this duty would have been reduced to 15 per cent to remain there practically for all time.

What is the
tariff in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think these articles are
free.

Absolutely free.
,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend will correct me if I am wrong. I try to carry as many of these matters in my head as I can, but I cannot carry them all.
That abolition of duty means something 'torn up.'

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The point I am making is that while my hon. friend from Red Deer is continually attacking our tariff, the tariff of the United States to-day, with the changes made to which he has referred, has a higher average of duty on dutiable commodities than has the tariff of Canada. I deal with the tariff as a whole because the hon. gentleman was dealing with it in that way and not with any particular duty. Mr. Underwood goes on:
To all intents and purposes, the Bill that is now presented to the House for its consideration provides an average of lower taxation than any Bill that has been presented in three-quarters of a century.
It follows, then, that the tariff of Canada which my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) is advising us to. revise-and in a year like this of all years-is lower than any tariff in the United States for three-quarters of a century. Yet my hon. friend from Red Deer tells us to look to the United States. Mr. Underwood proceeds:
The Wilson Bill carried an average rate of duty of 39.95 per cent. The Payne Bill carries an average rate of duty of 40.12 per cent, as compared with about 26 per cent that this Bill will carry.
My hon. friend has asked the Government to make an announcement as to certain matters brought to their attention by a delegation of farmers. There has been in Canada, I believe, ever since Conderera-tion and earlier, what I regard as a sound practice, namely, that announcements respecting the tariff are made only to Parliament, on the floor of Parliament and in the Budget speech. Personally, I have jealously guarded that rule. I consider it an eminently sound practice. I do not propose, and the Government does not propose, to depart from that rule, that custom, that sound practice. Whatever announcements the Government has to make respecting the tariff will not be made on ill-timed, unexpected occasions, but will be made in due course, at the proper time and in the Budget speech, and in the proper place, upon the floor of Parliament.
My right hon. leader (Mr. Borden) has called my attention to the language of

my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) in connection with this matter. He said:
I see the hon. member for York (Mr. McLeod) still gets lessons from that great coun-rty, because he quoted it in one particular in his speech to-night. Well, I looked to the great country to the south and I kept on looking, and now I turn to my hon. friends opposite and I say: Look at the great country to the south and what do you see? We see a great, simple and sincere man coming into office and cutting up protection and tearing its economic fallacies and false arguments into shreds and casting them to the four winds of heaven.
Notice the vigor and enthusiasm of that utterance.
That is'what I said-'fallacies and false arguments.'

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Scripta manet. Having
read the words of my hon. friend from Red Deer, I do not see any reason to change the view I expressed as to his utterance, unless he meant what he said about 'cutting up' protection to be taken in a merely figurative sense. I supposed that by 'cutting up' he meant making mincemeat of protection.
I fear that I have engaged the attention of the House for too long a time on this occasion; and I am very grateful to hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House for the close attention they have given me. I desire briefly to go over the heads of the subjects upon which I have touched. I referred to the naval question, and in this connection I want to ask my hon. friends opposite one question. In the speech of my right hon. friend I did not hear very much with regard to these two splendid battle units, one on the Atlantic and one on the Pacific, which were to be the immediate programme of hon. gentlemen opposite. I have not heard anything about the expenditure of $50,000,000 that would be required, $25,000,000 for each fleet, or the annual upkeep of $6,000,000, representing four per cent interest on $150,000,000. Perhaps the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) when dealing with this matter will tell us whether that is his programme at the present time. Will hon. gentlemen opposite engage in this expenditure, to say nothing of the enormous expense that would be involved in establishing armament manufactories in Canada in order that the ships composing those units may be constructed wholly in Canada, afterwards to be manned and operated by Canadians?
In so far as the attack upon our expenditure is concerned. I contend that, as compared wdth the record of hon. gentlemen opposite, this Government has been a prudent and economic government; that we have conserved the revenues of the Dominion, and that our surplus revenues have really been used to repair the mistakes made by our predecessors in office. In the fiscal years 1911-1912 our revenues were $168,000,000 and our expenses were kept within the moderate bounds of $143,000,000, giving a surplus over current, capital and special expenditure of $25,000,000. We used that $25,000,000, as I have said, for the purpose of repairing the blunder made by hon. gentlemen opposite in connection with the giving of the guarantee to the Grand Trunk Pacific. And yet hon. gentlemen opposite have the temerity to attack this Government for retrieving the errors which they themselves made, and for avoiding the loss of money and national credit which might have resulted from those mistakes. Considering the fact that we have devoted the greater portion of our expenditure to. the completion of enterprises promoted and inaugurated by hon. gentlemen opposite, I must say that their attitude is something like the unnatural parent denouncing the benefactor of his children. Any unusual financing we have done this year is not due to any programme initiated by this Government; it is but the aftermath of my right hon. friend's financial methods during his term of office, resulting in the expenditure of $22,000,000 with $10,000,000 more to come, to pay for the three per cent bonds guaranteed by the Government of Canada to the Grand Trunk Pacific. I hope therefore, that we shall hear no more about this question of lavish expenditure since we have taken office.
With regard to the cost of living, as I have said, the best remedy is to increase production, and we intend to do what we can, by the promotion of agriculture, to accomplish that most desirable end. The mew fiscal policy of my right hon. friend is simply a re-incarnation of reciprocity, which was pronounced against by the people of this country in 1911. As to the tariff, I have this to say to the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean). Prom time to time there are, of course, changing conditions which have to be met, but to consider as he suggests, a revision of the tariff downward in a year such as this-a year of slackening trade-and after such a period of financial stringency as that through which we have passed, would be to dislocate the industries of this country. So far as I know, there is no public opinion in

favour of a revision of tariff at this particular time. As I said in the beginning of my speech, we have gone through a very trying period; a long continued and severe depression. -But the light is now beginning to break; money is easier in the international centres, and that is the most hopeful sign to-day. Last fall was a good season for ploughing in Canada, and, with the promise of a favourable crop in the spring and the easing off of the money situation, this country should soon resume its wonted prosperity. No doubt we should go ahead cautiously for a time; it is very proper that we should, but the people of Canada should proceed also with confidence, and hon. gentlemen opposite should not, I think, discourage that confidence.
With regard to government expenditure, this Government has vast enterprises in hand, most of them inaugurated by our predecessors. We propose to carry out these public works; we propose to complete the great works to which we have committed ourselves. Extravagance is always to be deprecated, and I will never stand up in this House and defend the spending of money simply for the sake of spending it. That is unsound; on the other hand a policy of parsimony or timidity is more unsound. The middle course is the sound and . sensible policy from the standpoint of private or national finance, and that is the course we propose to pursue.
Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Edmonton); In attempting to offer some remarks to the House in this debate, I hope that my hon. friend the Finance Minister will not understand me as accepting on behalf of hon. gentlemen on this side the somewhat lengthy apology he has given for the position of the Government and its inaction in regard to the crisis which exists throughout the country. I was particularly interested in the remarks which my hon. friend had to offer on what at one moment he was pleased to call the new policy, and what at other moments he was pleased to designate as the old policy of the leader of the Opposition. I will not spend- further time in criticising that' part of my hon. friend's remarks, except to say that, carefully following them, it seemed to me that the latter half completely answered the first. Whereas he declared specifically in the beginning of his remarks that certain industries to the extent of hundreds of millions of capital and thousands of people would be in danger if the policy enunciated by the leader of the Opposition were adopted, in the latter half of his remarks he was at great trouble to prove
.
that by no possible change in the tariff could the cost of living be reduced.
The remarks of my hon. friend followed very closely the lines laid down in the Speech from the Throne, as well as in the addresses delivered in support of the position of the Government as there set out. This, I believe, is the first occasion in the history of the Canadian Parliament on which the Government has met Parliament with what can only be described as a purely ostrich policy. They have dropped, or forgotten, or ignored their policy regarding highways which at last session was one way of saving the country; they have ignored and dropped their policy regarding extensions of the Intercolonial railway ; have they ignored and dropped that great policy that was not only to save the country but also the empire, the naval question? And, Mr. Speaker, although they have relieved their minds of these important questions, in all the broad expanse of this Dominion of Canada, in its three thousand miles from ocean to ocean, with its seven millions of people and its rapidly growing interests, they have not found anything that requires the attention of Parliament at this session of sufficient importance to be mentioned in the Speech from the Throne, with the one exception alluded to by my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark), legislation that is automatically required by the British North America Act.
And even with regard to that they are late.

May I say, Mr. Speaker, that the attitude of the Government in the two previous sessions was that of the ostrich that runs around in a circle, but this session it is that of the ostrich which, having found no result from the circling process, sticks its head in the sand and thereby hopes to protect itself and to deceive its enemies. May I be pardoned if I suggest that the position is not graceful; it is not creditable, and it is decidedly vulnerable?
I think, Mr. Speaker, that our friends are under a misapprehension as to their responsibilities and as to the conditions in this case. I observe that so far from giving any intimation to the country that they have any views or intentions with regard to legislation, they have so far confined their allusions to expressions as to the policy of the party of the Opposition and of their honored leader. Far be it from me to in any way minimize the importance of these views and expressions by the leader of the Opposition and his followers in the House, but let me sug-

gest that the questions at issue before this country are to be decided by the Government on its responsibility and not on the views or opinions of the members of the Opposition, or even of the great leader of the Opposition. And may I suggest further that these gentlemen cannot escape from their responsibility, nor can this House afford the time to discuss or consider opinions that may have been expressed years ago; actions that were taken years ago; opinions that were proper and well supported at that time; actions that were taken for good reason and with sufficient results at that time. The fact of these actions and these reasons having been taken has no necessary bearing on present conditions. My hon. ftiends opposite in their attitude as expressed this session, bring to my mind the criticism of that great royal Bourbon family, of whom it was said: they never forgot anything and never learned anything. But our Mends of the Government have gone the Bourbons one better, for judging by their policy as expressed in the Speech from the Throne, they have forgotten everything, and judging of it as expressed in the speeches of their supporters delivered in this House, they do not seem to have learned anything.
I may be permitted to deal at some length with the situation of the country as it tis and with the duties and responsibilities of the Government in connection with that situation. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance have an easy way of dealing with it. They say: True, the times are hard; the times have been hard before and possibly will be hard again; wliat is that to us; why in 1907 times were hard and the then Government met Parliament with a paragraph in the Speech from the Throne parallel to the announcement which is inserted in the present speech. That is their idea of the fulfillment of their whole duty in a great national crisis. But let me remind them that the paragraph they have been good enough to quote from the speech of 1907 did not state that action had been taken Dy the Government of that day to meet wnat was on their showing a crisis parallel to that with which we are face to face to-day. My hon. friend knows well that on .the occasion of the depression of 1907 this Government did take such action to meet the conditions then existing; that when Parliament afterwards met they were criticised by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in words 6
to the effect that they might as well have taken crowbars and gone down to the treasury vaults as take the action they did. While gentlemen opposite say: Yes, times are hard, they were hard before and will be hard again, and we have nothing to do with it, the late Government took drastic action, action which was I believe outside the law, in order to meet the conditions, and they did meet them. And that was one reason why the country recovered as rapidly as it did on that occasion. I ask my hon. friends, charged with the direction of the public affairs of this country as they are, what warrant have they for presuming that matters will improve if they will only leave them alone? I am not prepared to say but that their judgment may be right in this particular instance, but I do say that they have no right to assume that that is the case. Nor have they any right to assume that they are doing their full duty that being the ease. I would ask my hon. friends, to what end does Parliament meet, for what purpose is the Government in office, if it is not to meet from day to day conditions as they arise, so that the people of this country will be benefited. If the Government has not that authority, if Parliament has not that responsibility, I ask, to what end are we here? Is the Government and Parliament a body whose sole duty is to levy taxes and to spend money? If that is my hon. friend's idea of the sole duty of Parliament, I take issue with him here and now, and so I think the country will.
I was struck by the stress that my hon. friend laid on the amount of money that was being spent in aid of agriculture, and particularly in agricultural education, by this Government as compared with expenditures by the previous Government. He brought out strongly the difference in the amounts spent, but I think it was when he made his claims as to the result of the expenditures by his Government that he excelled himself. We are to have a reduction in the cost of living without a reduction in the tariff. We are going to have a result that will mean many many millions of dollars to the people of this country by means of this expenditure. My hon. friends are spending about a million dollars a year more than their predecessors did in aid of agriculture. It is peculiar that our hon. friends who are so generous to agriculture, who expect such magnificent results from that generosity, should have up to date specifically refused, so far as the records show, every request that has been made by the author-



ized voice of agriculture in this country. I have here a report of a delegation which visited Ottawa recently. It comprised representatives from the Manitoba Grain Growers' Association, the Saskatchewan Grain Growers' Association, the United Farmers of Alberta, and the Ontario Grange. They met members of the Government, including the Premier, the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Public Works, the Postmaster General, the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of the Interior and the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Kemp), to whom they stated their views and desires. We aslc that all foodstuffs be placed on the free list, as we believe that the taxing of food is a crime against humanity.

In four years previous to January, 1913, fifty-six industrial mergers were negotiated, with an aggregate authorized capitalization of $456,938,266. The fifty-six amalgamations absorbed 248 individual companies. The aggregate capitalization of 206 of these individual companies was approximately $167,289,182, indicating that, whereas the people of "Canada had to provide dividends on $167,000,000, they have now to provide dividends on three times that amount. This enormous increase in capitalization is almost wholly made up of common stock, which admittedly represents very little real investment, being simply protection capitalized. A few outstanding illustrations are: The Canada Cement Company, Montreal, capitalized at $38,000,000, absorbed eleven companies with a total capital of $17,750,000 ; Ames-Holden & Mc-Cready, boots and shoes, capitalized at $11,- 500,000, absorbed two campanies, capital $3,500,000 ; Canada Cereal and Malting Company, capitalized at $3,250,000, absorbed eight companies with $809,000. capital; Dominion Can-ners, Hamilton, capitalized at $12,500,000, absorbed forty-five individual companies whose capital was given as $1,324,000. The total capitalization of manufacturers for the Dominion of Canada, according to the census returns, increased from $446,916,487 in 1901 to $1,247,58 9,609 in 1911; the ascertained surplus after deducting cost of raw material, wages, power, &c., from the gross revenues, showed an increase of net earnings on capitalization from 19.82 per cent in 1901 to 25 per cent in 1911.
I noted in the remarks, I think, of both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, that they could not understand how the farmer could receive a higher price and the consumer pay a lower price; but the farmers in this memorial throw some light on this subject. They say:
The average price paid farmers for tomatoes last year at Ontario factories was 30 cents per bushel. In some cases the price ran as low as 27J cents. It is stated that a bushel of these tomatoes will, under ordinary conditions, fill ten cans, the price of which to the consumer in western Canada is 20 cents per can.
I will place it before you if there is not ample room for an increase in the price for the producer and a decrease in the cost to the consumer. It is a puzzle for the Government to work out to show that the spread between the price received by the producer and the price paid by the consumer is not an inordinate one and does rot represent extortion upon either the producer or she consumer. That is their business, Mr. Speaker. To follow on:
That is to say, what the Ontario farmer gets 3 cents for (the Manitoba farmer pays 20 cents for. The manufacturers' census of 1911 shows the surplus earnings of canning factories of'

fruit and vegetables to be equal to 50 per cent, of the capital employed in the business. At the annual meeting of the Dominion Canners, Limited, in December last, it was given out that the net earnings of the company, after paying all fixed charges were 12 per cent on the common stock, which is supposed to represent nothing but water, and was selling on the stock exchange at S6.
Protection is intended to increase the cost of goods in the interest of the home manufacturer. It may be safely assumed that he will add the full amount of his protection to the selling price of his goods. Now the census and trade returns show in 1911 that for every dollar's worth of dutiable goods we imported, we manufactured $4 worth, consequently for every dollar we paid to the Government for revenue we paid four to the manufacturer.
I do not intend to traverse at any great length the question as to tne condition of the country as it is; but I think it is no harm to bring in the evidence of authorities that no one in the House or the country can dispute, for the purpose of showing that the Government of Canada have a responsibility and that the country calls upon them to discharge that responsibility. In the Ottawa Citizen, which is generally supposed to be a supporter of the Government of the day, and is published near enough to these halls to have a knowledge of the facts, I read as follows:
Unemployed in Canada.
Reports come from practically every center of population in Canada of large numbers of unemployed who are feeling the pinch of poverty. In the cities of the West there has been industrial distress for several months. The number of unemployed has been greatly in excess of the number to be expected by reason of the end of the demand for seasonal labour in the prairie provinces, and the consequent unemployment of the men so engaged. In British Columbia the same conditions have existed. In Regina, Sask., the situation is such that the police find it difficult to maintain order, it being feared for a time that martial law might have to be declared. That ominous institution, the soup kitchen, has made its appearance in this young and prosperous country. In Montreal hundreds of men stood in line at midnight to receive coffee and bread. In Toronto it is estimated that there are at present 15,000 men out of work, with the number on the increase.
In to-day's Ottawa Free Press, published here in the Capital city, I read the following:
Toronto Wants Work Started-Thirty Million Dollars Worth There to Help the City's Unemployed.
Toronto has adopted the plan resorted to in India in times of famine and has asked the Government for relief works. There are plans and appropriations for ten million dollars harbour improvements, for a new customs house, a new post office and the railways have plans for a new union station.

Altogether there is about thirty million dollars' worth of work in sight. Some has not been started and what has been commenced is being proceeded with in a leisurely fashion.
To-day-

To-day Mayor Hocken, Controller Church and Controller Simpson waited upon Hon. Robert Rogers, Hon. J. D. Reid and Hon. L. P. Pelle
