They also waited upon Chairman Drayton of the Railway Commission and asked him to make a peremptory order directing the railways immediately to begin work upon the union depot.
A sympathetic hearing was given the requests and it is understood that strong efforts will be made to meet the situation disclosed by the Toronto representatives.
The Minister of Finance read from the Labour Gazette of 1907 as to the conditions then. Wotild it be any harm to read from the Labour Gazette of December, 1913, as to conditions now?
Victoria.-Labour conditions were dull, not so good as during October, and much worse than the same month a year ago.
Nanaimo.-The labour situation shows very little change from last month, the city and district being full of idle men owing to the strike in the coal mines causing a general slackness in all branches of business.
Vancouver.-Industrial activity was less than it was at this time last year. Large numbers of unemployed men were walking the streets, and so serious is the situation that at a special meeting of the city council, held on November 21, a sum of money was voted for the purpose of opening up relief work for married men at $2.00 a day.
Lethbridge.-There was no improvement in labour conditions over last month. Farm help was not in demand. The city has been extending sewer and water connections, giving work to a number of men who otherwise would be idle. The building trades were dull. Work in the railroad yard is still being pushed ahead. Coal mining was very active, giving work to increasing number of men. All other branches of employment were dull.
And so on, practically all along the line.
I think, in view of all these quotations, it will not be argued that there is not a condition that requires the attention of the Government, if the Government has any purpose or business as such. If they are

to take the position, as they have so far taken it, that they have no responsibility; that it is only their business to levy the taxes and spend the money as they please, and wait for things to right themselves, it is desirable that that point should be nailed in the public mind, and that they should stand before the country of Canada as a Government in office and in power, not only unable, not only unwilling, but absolutely unknowing as to the conditions that require their attention.	.
Admitting that there are conditions that require attention, may I be permitted, Mr. Speaker, to bring before the House some information and views of my own as to how and why that condition exists, with a view of directing attention to the means necessary to secure its removal. My hon. friend has said, and has repeated and repeated that conditions in Canada are only as they are elsewhere throughout the world; that conditions are only as they were in 1907. What were the conditions in 1907? Everybody knows that the conditions in Canada were immediately, directly and unquestionably due to a condition of financial panic in the United States, such as that country had seldom seen, such as seldom occurred before and such as never has occurred since, and certainly such as does not exist now. At that time Canada Ijad suffered from serious failure in production. We had had a terribly severe winter in the West that wiped out possibly half of the range cattle, thus cutting off several million dollars in the winter of 1907-8. The summer was unfavourable. The harvest was late. The crop was damaged. Conditions were unfavourable in Canada; but still it was the panic in the United States that caused the financial stringency and made the difficulty that had to be coped with upon that occasion. To-day, as has been said and as has been repeated, Canada has harvested the largest crop that she has ever harvested. She has harvested it under the most favourable conditions; she has marketed it under the most favourable conditions, except as to price. There is no panic in the United States. Conditions of finance and labour in the United States to-day are better than they are in Canada. In Great Britain conditions not only are good but are magnificently good, both in regard to labour and finance. Canada is the country to-day that stands by herself as the country of depression, in the face of the most magnificent crop it ever harvested. In 1907, in the face of a bad winter, in the face of a bad summer, Canada still stood as the best of the countries within our immediate range, as far as finances were concerned. There is
,
no comparison between the conditions in 1907 and the conditions of to-day.
Just as the conditions of 1907 had a cause, which was the panic in the United States, so the conditions of to-day have a cause, and the conditions of to-day call for a remedy. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. White) repeated and repeated that the cure for the present condition, for the high cost of living, for the financial stringency, was increased production, more people on the land, and more production from the land. There is no doubt that is the cure; but my hon. friend did not give us any indication as to how he was going to apply the cure, and he did not even hold out the idea that he was in any way responsible for its application. Let me point out how the disease has come about, as I understand it. Enough has been said to demonstrate beyond question that, when all the great financiers, all the great industrial institutions and all the great transportation organizations are set on one side, the source of the wealth of Canada is the land; and the progress of its wealth is absolutely dependent upon the progress of the cultivation of the land, which again is contained in the agricultural development of the prairie provinces. If we have had increasing prosperity in Canada, we have had it because there has been increasing production in our prairie west.
My hon. friend the Minister of Finance almost shed tears over the fact that the late Government had practically ignored the agricultural industry. Does my hon. friend know that under the late Government, if I may quote from the material which was presented to himself, amongst others, by the delegates from the western provinces and Ontario, the acreage under crop in the three western provinces in the year 1901 was about 2,500,000 acres, and in 1911 it was over 17,000,000 acres? This agriculture that the late Government did not encourage increased seven-fold during ten years under the administration of the late Government. I ask my hon. friend, has he any hope or prospect that it will increase seven-fold under his administration, with the aid even of his $1,000,000 a year for agricultural education? It was that increase in cultivation in the West that made Canada; that built the railroads, that started the factories, that gave dividends to the banks; that created the great commercial houses; that did whatever has been done that amounted to any-

thing in those years. It was the foundation of it all. The homesteader on the prairie with his yoke of oxen or his team of horses and his plough, who has been held up to obloquy as the miner of wheat, who has been advised by my hon. friend to go into mixed farming in order to save the country, this was the man who made Canada. What treatment has he had at the hands of my hon. friend and his friends since they came into office? They will educate him. Yes. But he needs something more than education. I would like to say to my hon. friend that the western farmer is fairly well educated in what constitutes his own business. The fact that he has done what he has done is all the evidence that is necessary upon that point.
Let me call the attention of the House back to the year 1911, the year when my hon. friend took office. There were unfortunate weather conditions at that time. There was a damaged crop. There was a grain blockade. I had the honour to bring to the attention of the House facts . and figures, which were not denied in any degree, showing that the direct loss to the wheat farmers of the prairie west that year, because of the grain blockade then existing, which did not need to exist, which should not have existed, and which would not have existed if this Government had taken proper action, was not less than $10,000,000 in cold cash.
In the year 1912 there was an-
10 p.m. other occasion of unfavourable harvesting conditions, another year of late forwarding of the crop, another year of partial grain blockade. I shall not trouble the House with figures; but, if my memory serves me right, while in the year 1911 the condition became so bad and the facts were impressed so strongly upon the attention of the Government, that they did finally take certain action, in the year 1912, as far as I recall, the grain blockade existed without any relief at the hands of the Government of the day.
The farmer of the West does not raise wheat for fun or for the sake of its appearance. He raises it to sell, and upon the price that he gets for that wheat depends the possibility of his continuing in business. If he makes a profit, he stays in business, let the profit be never so small. If he does not make a profit, what happens to the banker or the manufacturer or the merchant, happens to the farmer; the
sheriff gets him; he goes out of business. One of the factors affecting the price of wheat to the farmer is the cost of transportation. The distance from the wheat field to the ultimate market is stupendous. Toll is taken at every point, by the receiving elevator, the railroad, the terminal elevator, the steam-boat over the lakes, the receiving elevator again, the railroad, the ocean elevator, the ocean vessel, and again the ocean elevator.
We have been told at great length in this House about the steamship combine on the Atlantic ocean and how that has undulv increased the rates of freight upon the western farmers' wheat, causing the depression in prices. There is no doubt that combine has taken place. There is no doubt that fact has materially affected and limited the profit of the farmer in the West. Ocean transportation is not within the jurisdiction of this House. It is a magnificent subject for declamation, and speeches made on that subject look well on ' Hansard,' but they do not mean anything. They do not get anywhere; they do not take anything off the rates of transportation, and they do not add anything to the price of the farmers' wheat. But there is a link in that line of transportation which is within the jurisdiction of this Government and Parliament of Canada, that link which extends from Fort William at the head of Lake Superior to such port at the foot of Georgian bay or other lake ports as may occur. This is a link of transportation that is within the jurisdiction of this Parliament, and what has taken place on the ocean has taken place on the lakes. A lake merger has been formed and the rate of freight across the lakes has cost the farmer from one to two or even three cents a bushel during this and the previous year. What have our friends on the other side done in that regard? Everybody will remember that last session a Bill was before the House to make provision for an increased capitalization for the express purpose of giving that merger firmer control of the situation, and facts advertised in the newspapers, stated the reason for the forming of the merger as being for the purpose of levying toll upon the transportation of wheat. When the question was brought to the attention of the Government, they were asked to take action. Votes were taken upon it in this House and what was the answer? They have money to spend for the education of the farmer, but they have no attention to give to secure for him a fair price for his product, or to protect

him against the rapacity and extortion of mergers and combines. We have this year 150,000,000 bushels of wheat marketed up to this time. The price of every bushel that is actually marketed is based upon the export price. That is to say, the price of every bushel of that 150,000,000 bushels has been subjected to a reduction by the amount of the extortion of the lake merger, an average of two cents a bushel, as I am credibly informed. That means that there has been taken out of the farmers' pockets this year, out of the pockets of the raisers of wheat, in a winter when the price is abnormally low, $3,000,000 with the knowledge and consent and assistance of thiis Government and their majority in Parliament. And they are going to save the country by the amount of education they propose to give the farmers. They are teaching the farmer a good many things he did not know a few years ago, but I think that the farmer will teach them something when the next opportunity occurs.
I have told the House that the farmers of the West lost $10,000,000 on the crop of 1911, I have not given the figures for the crop of 1912, but I have given $3,000,000 with regard to the crop of 1913. What lis the result? The result is that while the farmer some years ago was farming at a profit; while farming was increasing from year to year, it having increased from two and a half to seventeen million acres in ten years, it has practically been at a standstill during these three years. The lincrease of production which was the gold mine of Canada has not occurred in those years, and for that reason. Immigration into Canada has increased, but homestead entries have decreased; there were 10,000 less entries in the year ended March 31, 1913, than there were in the year ended March 31, 1911. This is how my hon. friends opposite have been pushing people on to the land; this is how they have been encouraging (increased cultivation and helping to bring down the cost of living.
I have read from the memorial of the farmers' delegation a quotation showing the burden that has been placed upon the whole of the consumers of this country, and upon the farmer more than any other, by the capitalization of protection and the formation of mergers. I have mentioned the canners' combine, which (increased to the consumers of the West the cost of the product of that combine, a necessary of life in that country, by seventy per cent.
,
Again we are told that the farmers need education; what I say is that the farmer needs a living chance; he needs a fair opportunity, and it is for this Government to meet conditions as they arise and to give the farmer the opportunity to which he is entitled, and of which if he gets it, he will take full advantage for the good of himself and the good of the country.
But what has that to do with the conditions of finance and labour in Canada as a whole? I said in the beginning, and I say again, that as the increase of cultivation in the West was the gold mine upon which the increase of Canada's prosperity was built in the last ten yeirs, so when that gold mine ceases to increase in production, will the prosperity built upon it cease to increase in corresponding degree. If the farmers in the West do not make a profit, they cannot buy the products of the factories of the East. If there are factories closed up in the province of Ontario to-day-and there are; if there are others running on half time and on reduced wages-and there are; if collections are difficult and	money	is
tight, it is in a large measure because the farmers of the western prairie have not been dealt with fairly or justly by this Government since it came into office. Hon. gentlemen opposite may say ' this does not concern us.' I say it does concern them. When there is a lack of employment, when there is a lack of business, it is for the Government to search out the cause and apply the remedy. I give them in a large measure the cause; I give them the remedy. Give us favourable conditions in the West in regard to transportation, in regard to the tariff and in regard to land conditions generally, and we will give you increased cultivation; we will give you increased production; we will give you increased prosperity. But we cannot make bricks without straw. If you tie our hands; if you burden our backs; if we must pay excessive tolls to the railway companies, the steamship companies, the canners' combine, and every kind, shape and form of business interest that can claim the protection of this Government, then you cannot get favourable results. The resultwill be that you must face the same condition that faced this country during the unfortunate period when the predecessors of the late Government were in office, when the same policy as the one which my hon. friend has vaunted here to-night was the policy of the Government, and when the country wound up in the same condition as that

towards which it is rapidly going to-day.
My hon. friend says we cannot change the tariff in an era of hard times. I ask him when should we change the tariff, if not during a period of hard times ? Why are times hard ? Because-I am speaking now to the Minister of Finance-because people spend more than they have; because they need to get more money and to spend less. Then surely it is obvious, even to a minister of finance, that to give the benefit of wider markets to the great productive interests of the country and to lessen the taxation paid by the whole people would surely be a me'asurable remedy for the shortage of money. But my hon. friend says no. He says that at this time we cannot do anything; we must wait until, I suppose, times get better. I take my hon. friend at his word; he has declared the policy of his Government, and I desire to register my strongest opposition to him.
I have a clipping here which I wish to place before the House, following up the idea that the burdens which are carried by the western farmer and by the whole of the consumers of this country are unreasonable, that they have tended to bring about the present condition, and that they call for remedy at the hands of the Government. It will be said that the late Government did not apply any remedy. That is true. There were many things that the late Government did not do. If that Government had done everything that ought to have been done, there would be no need for this Parliament. I quote from the Canadian Grocer of Nov. 29, 1912:
There are many staple lines of groceries that no one except a legitimate retailer can purchase,-
This was in 1912, it will be noted. That was not under the late Government; this is an announcement made while hon. gentlemen opposite were in office.
*-and they must also he bought from legitimate wholesale groceries at prices set by the manufacturer. These include well-known brands of sugar, cereals, syrups, canned goods, soups, etc.
That is to say, the ordinary necessaries of life, articles of food and of the greatest utility, we are buying in an absolutely restricted market and at prices fixed, not by the law of supply and demand, but by the avarice of those who control that market.	.
My hon. friend says that the tariff would not make any difference. Well, as I have said, he answered that theory himself so well that it would be out of place for me to
spend any time upon it. I do not know that the tariff would make all the difference, but I do submit-and it is a well-known fact-that it is the foundation upon which the combines build their arrangements, and the taking awajr of the tariff would be the first step, and the most necessary step, towards breaking the combines. My hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) reminds me that I am beating the air in making this argument to the House.
I call upon my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, who has already proved absolutely, not by words but by acts, the truth of my argument. He did this when he took off half the duty on cement. Why did he do that? Because there was a combine. He then 'believed that the reduction of the duty would have a beneficial effect in favour of the consumers of cement. And he was right; the place where he was wrong was when he put the duty back.
On the question of the high cost of living and the advice of my hon. friend that we all go out and raise steers*, let me give the House some information from a point of view that I have not gathered from the newspaper criticisms of the situation that I have seen. There seems to be a general idea running through the newspaper comments that beef is scarce because prices are high. Now beef is scarce because the price a few years ago was so low. The arrangements as to marketing beef in Canada were such that the price was forced down to the lowest possible margin, and hundreds of people went out of keeping cattle because the keeping of cattle did not pay. The increase in the price, of beef will mean an increase in * the quantity of beef in due course; and my hon. friend the Minister of Finance if he will only not shut our beef out of the American market, can depend upon it that the price that we have received because of our access to that market will insure an adequate supply of beef in due course. In 1908 the average price of beef cattle in Winnipeg was $3.53 per 100 pounds. In 1913, the average price was $6.07 per 100 pounds. The price nearly doubled in that time. And to-day the price in Chicago is $7.50 per 100 pounds. Now I need not labour the argument:-that in the case of the farmer as in the case of every other business man it is the profit on the business that enables him to carry it on; that if he does not make a profit he cannot remain in business; and that when the price of his wheat or his cattle is forced down so that he does not make a profit, he cannot pay his debts, he is forced out of business, and production is

reduced to a corresponding degree. Give the farmer a profit and the farmer will give you the production. If you are not going to let the farmer have a profit; if you are going to ba k the railroad companies against him, if you are going to back the canners' combine -against him, if you are going to back the bank against him, if you are going to back every interest that comes along against him, you are going to put him out of business and you are going to get the results you have got.
That reminds me:	At the last
session of Parliament we had a revision of the Bank Act. An amendment was inserted to make provision tlqit banks might lend money on wheat. When the Bill was before the House the proposal that banks should be allowed to lend money on cattle was brought to the attention of the Minister of Finance. It was considered advisable that there should be the same privilege in regard to cattle that was given in regard to wheat. Did my hon. friend make this Chamber ring with his assertions as to the desirability of the farmer going into mixed farming, and everybody going out to raise cattle and hogs, and that every assistance that legislation could give would be given? Not at all. He stood in his place and absolutely refused the request made. He kept out of the Bill the provision that would permit the banks to advance money on cattle on a parallel with the advance upon wheat-another instance of the encouragement that my hon. friend gives to the farmer in the prosecution of his business. He is willing to educate the farmer; he is not willing to lef him do business in a business way.
I take issue with my hon. friend on his view with regard to the inadvisability of action being taken by the Government at the present time to remedy existing conditions. I say that if ever action was necessary it is now; I say it is demanded at this session of Parliament and without further delay. If we must wait for the Budget, then the Budget should come down; if there is to be any remedy provided by the Budget that remedy should be applied at once. So far as the crop of the past year is concerned, it is out of the farmers' hands now and the price of wheat, as will be seen, is gradually going up. The Finance Minister and his Government could have put into the pockets of the farmers in the West as a part of the price of that crop-and could have put it in the pockets of the farmers of the West by the stroke of a pen-anywhere from $4,000,000 to $8,000,000. That would have been encouragement. All he had to do was
.
to repeal the duty on wheat; what he half did in regard to cement he could have all done in regard to wheat. The difference in prices between Winnipeg and Minneapolis on the same quality of wheat has run anywhere from three cents to six cents a bushel this year; to-day it stands at about six cents. Had the Finance Minister been minded to give the Western farmer the benefit of free access to the Minneapolis market, he could, I am advised, have done it without waiting for Parliament. He did not have to wait for Parliament in the case of the reduction of the cement duties; he did not need to await Parliament to reduce the duty on wheat. And, if he had done so he knew there would be no doubt about his receiving the sanction of Parliament. Today the farmers of the western country have from 85,000,000 to 88,000,000 less money than they would have had if the Minister of Finance and his colleagues in the Ministry had simply put pen to paper. I ask you, would not that have made some difference in the present financial condition of this country? Would the distribution of that $5,000,000 throughout the prairie West not have saved many a farmer from bankruptcy; would it not have kept many a man in this poor year out of the hands of the sheriff? I say it would. I say it wpuld have helped to keep open the factories of Ontario; it would have helped collections by the banks and commercial houses, and it would have helped every interest in this whole Dominion. But the Minister of Finance has a policy; it is the National Policy, he says, of 1878. He is for high tariff and he won't admit that a change of tariff will make any difference in the cost of living, and I suppose he will not admit that any change in the tariff can Inake any difference in the price of wheat. His Government will have to stand on that and they will be judged by it. My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) told him what had happened in the case of oats, and that because the United States reduced the duty on oats to six cents a bushel we have been able to send many millions of bushels of oats to that country. That saved the situation in regard to oats. We were selling oats at from 16 to 18 cents a bushel. That did not pay the cost of production. The Minister of Finance was raised on a farm and he knows it did not. It was the reduction in tne United States duty which enabled us to ship some of our surplus oats to the United States that saved the situation so far as oats is concerned, and even on what we did ship we had to pay the six cents a bushel, because it was not the United States consumer who paid it,

it was the Canadian producer who paid. And yet the Minister of Finance says this_ is not the time for us to make changes
in	the	tariff,	when	the prairiefarmer	will be	able	to buy hisfruit	at a price	less	the amountof	the	duty;	this	is not the
time to make changes in the tariff or ac-<ept the provisions of the reciprocity arrangement and enable the Canadian apple grower to sell in cities ot hundreds of thousands, where he is now restricted to cities of tens of thousands? Surely, if ever there was a time to call for energetic action on the part of any government; if ever there was a time that called for action that would reduce the burden upon the people of this country, that time is now. The occasion calls for the Government; it is for them to respond or not. They have had their opportunity; they have declared their policy; there is nothing in [DOT]sight for this country; the Government is in the hands of the men who put them there to do their bidding and the country may save itself so far as they care.
I do not know that I would be justified in closing without making a reference to a subject that has been mentioned by all of the speakers on the Address up to the present time, namely, the naval question. I do not speak of the naval policy of the Government, because, however they may have a tariff policy, aparently they have no naval policy. I will not delay the House at any great length on this point, but I will say this; the right lion, the Prime Minister, and his colleagues who have spoken, and his supporters, and his press in the country, have been vociferously claiming that their naval policy was actuated by and founded on the principle of Imperial loyalty; the idea of strengthening this great empire which stands for liberty throughout the world. It is strange, it is pasing strange, that conditions have so changed in such a short time that that which only a year ago called for a definite policy and for a vast expenditure, and called so loudly and insistently that it was necessary to deprive this House of its traditional and necessary privileges; it is strange that the same Government comes to this House now and has not a word to say in regard to the policy of naval defence. May I say that, in my humble judgment, if they are to claim credit for a sound imperialism, if they are to claim credit for a patriotic Canadianism, they will have to make some declaration before this session closes in regard to a permanent naval policy; a permanent policy of Canadian naval defence, having regard to Canada's position and Canada's imperial obligations.
These gentlemen have made high claims for themselves. They have gone out of their way to heap discredit upon the position and views of their opponents. They have raked the dictionary for words to express the depth of their loyalty and the urgency with which they were prepared to rush to the rescue of the empire. To-day their desire to rush to the empire's rescue has degenerated into a quarrel with the Upper House of this Parliament; and while a year ago they were declaiming about the sacrifices they were prepared to make in the interests of the empire, to-day they are satisfied with making threats against the Upper Chamber. I need not say that such action on their part is not only improper, it is unparliamentary, and may I suggest that it is even unconstitutional. I submit that it is unheard of, that the motives of the Upper Chamber of this Parliament should be called in question in this House. By what right does the Premier of Canada say that the Upper Chamber, a body co-ordinate with this House, does not act on its own motion and for its own good reasons. I say that such a statement as the Premier made here is improper and to my mind unparliamentary and should not have been made under those conditions. The Senate of Canada has a certain responsibility given it by the Imperial Parliament. Because it has seen fit to discharge this responsibility according to the judgment of a majority of its members it is to be called in question in this House, to be threatened as it was threatened by the Prime Minister. That is not parliamentary	government	in	its propersense. Everybody knows that a threat made against the Senate is an absurdity. There are no means whereby that threat can be carried out, even with the high authority of the leader of this Government. Our constitution comes from the Imperial Parliament and it is only there that	our	constitution
can be revised. If there is to be a question before the Canadian people as to the right or wrong of the Senate, then I say it is for the Government, if they have a policy that they believe in, and that the Senate does not believe in, to get their views before the country by bringing forward that policy just as often as they have an opportunity. If they had believed that they were right and that the Senate was wrong they would have done it and they would have had their Highways Bill, their Branch Lines
no

Bill and the Naval Bill before the House at this session. But they knew they were wrong and that the Senate was right, and they did not dare to come before the court of public opinion again with that legislation. They preferred to keep in the background, to send out threats and insinuations, depending upon taking the country by surprise, upon misrepresentation and lack of understanding on the part of the people at the next general election. If these measures are right let them be brought forward and threshed out before the people of the country. We on this side of the House are prepared to stand behind the position that we took and I am satisfied that the Senate will again take what action its judgment may commend to it, when the occasion arises. But aside from the quarrel between the Senate and the Government, I say the Government cannot evade the responsibility that properly rests upon them to provide for the naval defence of Canada as a part of the British Empire. The combination between Nationalists and Imperialists which was to be carried through under cover of an emergency policy has now no excuse, and if those who claim Imperial loyalty are loyal, now is the time to show it by bringing before Parliament proposals for a permanent naval policy. The fact that the Government have not done so is evidence that they dare not and shows that the claims they made of loyalty to the empire are empty and were made under false pretenses. They have the opportunity and they are not able to make good. They have been in power for two years. They have tried to pass the question over by an emergency policy. They were not able to do it. They are not now bringing forward a permanent policy. Let their present position be contrasted with the position they held at the last session when they came to Parliament with great declarations of imperial loyalty and with great propositions for the salvation of the empire. To-day they dare not even say they have a policy that.will have any effect either for the safety of Canada or for the empire. I can only repeat what I said in the beginning that never was a Parliament of Canada met by a Government with such a lack of policy and such a lack of proposals as upon this occasion. As at the last session they hoped to defend themselves by a policy of silence, so now they hope to protect themselves by having no policy at all. But I say that in this country of 7,000,000 people, of 3,000 miles in distance, a country with problems that are growing from day to day and demanding solution, I say that in this ,
country they cannot satisfy public opinion by a policy of seeing nothing, knowing nothing or doing nothing.

I was not in when the iron, member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) was referring to canned goods, but I understand that he stated that canned goods have increased in price 70 per cent in the last five years.
That is what I understood.

You are entirely wrong. Canned goods are cheaper to-day than they have been for five years. Tomatoes are 30 per cent, cheaper than they were a year ago, peas about 25 per cent cheaper, and corn about 10 per cent cheaper.
